spec.title: Ivory Crown
spec.subtitle: An ivory marble tomb beside the Yamuna, born of love and empire.

chapters.label: CHAPTER 01 · FOUNDATION
chapters.heading: A riverbank cleared for a dream of marble.
chapters.subheading: The ground was leveled and filled against seepage.
chapters.body: The site on the right bank of the Yamuna was excavated, filled with dirt and leveled fifty metres above the river. Brick and lime mortar formed the footings, while a massive brick scaffold mirrored the tomb. More than twenty thousand artisans worked under a board of architects led by Ustad Ahmad Lahori.

chapters.label: CHAPTER 02 · MAUSOLEUM
chapters.heading: White marble rises, inlaid with distant stones.
chapters.body: Completed in 1648, the tomb is veneered with ivory-white marble sourced from Makrana. Semi-precious stones, including jade, crystal, turquoise, lapis lazuli, sapphire and carnelian, were inlaid across its surface. Red sandstone forms the surrounding mosque and guest house. The complex spans seventeen hectares, bounded on three sides by a crenellated wall and laid out in formal gardens.

chapters.label: CHAPTER 03 · LEGACY
chapters.heading: A world heritage jewel endures through centuries.
chapters.body: Designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1983, the Taj Mahal is hailed as a masterpiece of Mughal architecture. It draws more than five million visitors each year and was named a winner of the New Seven Wonders of the World in 2007. The complex remains administered by the Archaeological Survey of India and stays open from before sunrise to before sunset.
